title: Global Financial Stability Report, April 2026 (and Spring Meetings press briefing)
date_evidence: Press Briefing Transcript: Global Financial Stability Report, Spring Meetings 2026 ... April 14, 2026
key_claim: Stretched valuations and concentration, particularly in AI-related firms, raise downside risks in equity markets; some firms along the AI value chain have increasingly relied on circular financing; data centres are becoming a large part of global commercial real estate, raising obsolescence questions; private credit leverage and interconnectedness flagged.
verbatim_quote: Stretched valuations and concentration, particularly in AI-related firms, raise downside risks in equity markets. Some firms along the AI value chain have increasingly relied on circular financing.
notes: Tier 1 multilateral. Names circular financing and AI-valuation concentration as financial-stability concerns.

title: FSB warns on private credit vulnerabilities (Report on Vulnerabilities in Private Credit)
date_evidence: meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-05-06T06:00+00:00" ... FSB warns on private credit vulnerabilities 6 May 2026
key_claim: Private credit has grown to an estimated $1.5-2.0 trillion at end-2024 and is concentrated in a few sectors, notably technology; valuation opacity and reliance on private ratings can amplify stress; direct bank exposures of around $220 billion of drawn and undrawn credit lines to private credit funds, with commercial estimates of $270-500 billion; AI firms increasingly turning to private lenders to fund datacentres.
verbatim_quote: Private credit has grown to an estimated $1.5-2.0 trillion at end-2024 and is concentrated in a few sectors, notably technology. Direct bank exposures of around $220 billion of drawn and undrawn credit lines to private credit funds, with commercial estimates of $270-500 billion. AI firms increasingly turning to private lenders to fund datacentres.
notes: Tier 1 standard-setter. Concentration in technology and bank interlinkage figures are core quantification anchors.

title: Financial Policy Committee Record - April 2026 (meeting of 27 March 2026)
date_evidence: The Bank of England published a record of the Financial Policy Committee meeting that took place on 27 March 2026 on 1 April 2026.
key_claim: The FPC identified vulnerabilities in risky credit markets, including private credit, as having shown signs of worsening; AI-related risks likely to increase, potentially rapidly, amid growing intent to deploy advanced AI; Committee asked for further work on agentic AI in payments and financial markets.
verbatim_quote: Vulnerabilities in risky credit markets, including private credit, have shown signs of worsening. AI-related risks likely to increase, potentially rapidly, amid growing intent to deploy advanced AI.
notes: Tier 1 regulator. Establishes that a G7 macroprudential authority is monitoring private credit + AI as linked risks.

title: Financial Stability Review, May 2026
date_evidence: www.ecb.europa.eu (c) 27 May 2026 Financial Stability Review May 2026
key_claim: An AI investment boom increasingly financed by private credit could expose euro-area insurers and pension funds to material second-round losses if technology returns disappoint; in an ECB stress scenario pension funds would lose 5-6% of total assets and insurers around 4%, with bank losses contained at no more than 1.3% of equity; US private credit reached about $1.4 trillion at end-2024, a scale the ECB compared to the $1.5 trillion US subprime mortgage market; high concentration of private credit in IT and software is of particular concern.
verbatim_quote: An AI investment boom increasingly financed by private credit could expose euro-area insurers and pension funds to material second-round losses if technology returns disappoint. In an ECB stress scenario pension funds would lose 5-6% of total assets and insurers around 4%, with bank losses contained at no more than 1.3% of equity. US private credit reached about $1.4 trillion at end-2024, a scale the ECB compared to the $1.5 trillion US subprime mortgage market.
notes: Tier 1 regulator. The subprime comparison and stress-scenario loss figures are the strongest quantification anchors in the evidence base.

title: Moody's flags $662 billion risk at the heart of the data center build-out by just 5 companies
key_claim: The top five US hyperscalers had amassed $969 billion in total undiscounted future data-centre lease commitments as of end-2025; $662 billion of that is for leases not yet commenced and therefore off balance sheet under GAAP, equivalent to 113% of the five firms' most recent adjusted debt; AI hardware has a useful life of just four to six years, pushing firms toward shorter leases backstopped by off-balance-sheet residual value guarantees (e.g. Meta's $28 billion RVG recorded as no liability).
verbatim_quote: The top five US hyperscalers had amassed $969 billion in total undiscounted future data-centre lease commitments as of end-2025. $662 billion of that is for leases not yet commenced and therefore off balance sheet under GAAP, equivalent to 113% of the five firms' most recent adjusted debt. AI hardware has a useful life of just four to six years. Meta's $28 billion residual value guarantee recorded as no liability.
notes: Structural anchor (25 Feb 2026, ~3 months). Analytical source is Moody's Ratings credit research (analysts David Gonzales, Alastair Drake); classified Tier 2 on that basis though accessed via Fortune. Canonical quantification of the off-balance-sheet layer.

title: Tokenmaxxing is over. That's because it never measured what really counts to see ROI from AI
date_evidence: Tokenmaxxing is over... By Jeremy Kahn May 28, 2026
key_claim: Enterprises are increasingly questioning whether AI spending is producing measurable return, with the 'tokenmaxxing' growth thesis giving way to scrutiny of ROI - the demand assumption on which the financing build-out depends.
notes: Tier 3 journalism. Used as directional evidence for the ROI-disappointment trigger and the counter-argument.

title: Starbucks quietly retired its AI agent just months after deployment after it miscounted coffee shop inventories and slowed down baristas
date_evidence: Starbucks quietly retired its AI agent... By Sasha Rogelberg May 28, 2026
key_claim: A named enterprise (Starbucks) retired a deployed AI agent within months because it miscounted inventory and slowed staff - a concrete data point that deployment ROI is lagging the capital being committed to AI infrastructure.
notes: Tier 3 journalism. Corroborates the deployment-reality gap underpinning the disconfirming-signal and counter-argument sections.
